analysis.one_liner: Lets workers on strike collect unemployment benefits after two weeks.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would let striking workers draw unemployment benefits, has sat without action in the House Ways and Means Committee since its introduction in September 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, workers on strike generally cannot collect unemployment benefits in most states, because they are employed and because they are not available for other work. This bill would change federal law so that a striker is treated as unemployed for benefits purposes, with payments starting 14 days after a strike begins, immediately if the employer locks workers out or hires permanent replacements, and immediately when the dispute ends. It would also exempt strikers from the requirement that unemployment recipients be available for work.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who go on strike or are locked out, and their unions. Strikes often fail because workers exhaust savings within weeks; a benefits check after two weeks, or immediately in a lockout, would let them hold out longer. Workers idled indirectly by a nearby labor dispute would also qualify.

how_it_helps.text: A striker would be treated 'as though such individual were unemployed' for unemployment compensation purposes, rather than being disqualified because they still have a job.
Benefits would start 14 days after a strike begins, or sooner if the employer locks workers out, hires permanent replacement workers, or the dispute ends.
Strikers would be exempt from the Social Security Act requirement that unemployment claimants be available for work, removing a second common disqualification.
Workers unable to work as an indirect result of a labor dispute would also be covered.

analysis.who_pays: State unemployment insurance funds, which are financed by payroll taxes on employers. Because those taxes are experience-rated, employers involved in labor disputes would bear more of the cost over time, and the change would raise benefit outlays during strikes nationwide.

drawbacks.text: The bill guarantees benefits during a strike without a work-search requirement, which critics argue changes unemployment insurance from a safety net for the jobless into support for a bargaining tactic, and could make strikes longer and more common.

The added benefits would be paid out of state unemployment trust funds financed by employer payroll taxes, adding costs to a system that many states had to borrow from the federal government to prop up after past downturns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gain is substantial: the financial fragility of striking families is a main reason unions lose long disputes, and this would materially rebalance bargaining power at a modest per-claimant cost. The honest counterweight is that unemployment insurance was not designed for this, states would administer an expanded program financed by employer taxes, and opponents would say the public is being asked to fund one side of a private bargaining fight. The bill does nothing to address the underlying dispute; it only changes who absorbs the income loss while it continues.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it since September 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Norcross and 23 original cosponsors introduced the bill in the House on September 8, 2025.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which is the only action recorded since.
As of the latest action history, the committee has held no markup, reported no bill, and the House has not voted on it.
The bill would amend the Internal Revenue Code and the Social Security Act to make strikers eligible for unemployment compensation and exempt them from the work-availability requirement.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet, because nothing has happened beyond referral. Employers facing strikes are better off for now in that the status quo, under which strikers get no benefits, remains in place while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, for now, via the status quo

for.name: Rep. Donald Norcross
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend unemployment benefits to striking workers.

for.name: 52 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Ocasio-Cortez, Jayapal, Casar, and Dingell.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 8, 2025 and has taken no further action; no markup, hearing, or floor scheduling has been recorded.

sides.party_line_note: All 53 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, and the bill sits in a Republican-chaired committee.

industries.note: The bill would remove a key economic advantage employers hold in strikes: strikers running out of money. It would also add to their unemployment insurance tax burden through experience rating during labor disputes.
Longer, better-funded strikes strengthen unions' bargaining position, which is the bill's stated purpose of 'empowering striking workers.'
States would administer expanded benefits during labor disputes, raising payouts from employer-financed trust funds, though the federal conforming amendments would make the rules uniform nationwide.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and no committee action months after referral, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or floor vote in this Congress; the usual path for a bill at this stage is to remain in committee until the session ends.
